blocks.text: 1.Type 1 diabetes: autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells, resulting in absolute insulin deficiency.
2.Type 2 diabetes: insulin resistance with progressive beta-cell dysfunction.
3.Gestational diabetes: diabetes diagnosed during pregnancy that is not clearly overt pre-existing diabetes.
**Exam pearl:** Type 1 diabetes can occur at any age. Do not diagnose diabetes type based on age or body habitus alone.

items.text: Unexplained weight loss, particularly in type 1 diabetes.

blocks.text: **Exam pearl:** Weight loss despite increased appetite is particularly suggestive of uncontrolled diabetes with significant insulin deficiency.
Diabetes can be diagnosed using any of the following accepted laboratory criteria:

rows: ≥11.1 mmol/L with classic symptoms or hyperglycaemic crisis

items.text: Fasting means no caloric intake for at least 8 hours.
In an asymptomatic patient, an abnormal result generally requires confirmation with repeat testing or another diagnostic test.
HbA1c may be unreliable in conditions affecting red-cell lifespan, some haemoglobin variants, pregnancy and certain anaemias.
Plasma glucose criteria are preferred when HbA1c is unreliable.

subsections.subsection_title: 4. Causes and risk factors of Type 2 diabetes – DIABETES

rows: Diet high in energy and refined carbohydrates
Body fat excess, particularly central obesity

blocks.text: Other risk factors include previous gestational diabetes, polycystic ovary syndrome and hypertension.
**Exam pearl:** Family history, central obesity and insulin resistance are important clues, but type 2 diabetes can also occur in people who are not overweight.

subsections.subsection_title: 5. Chronic complications of diabetes – MICRO and MACRO

items.text: Coronary artery disease and myocardial infarction.

blocks.text: Other important diabetic foot problems include neuropathy, deformity, infection and Charcot arthropathy.
DKA results from insulin deficiency and increased counter-regulatory hormones, causing hyperglycaemia, ketone production and metabolic acidosis.
Other triggers include pancreatitis, stroke, trauma, surgery and certain medications, including SGLT2 inhibitors.

rows: Blood beta-hydroxybutyrate ≥3.0 mmol/L, or significant urine ketones if blood testing unavailable
pH below 7.3 and/or bicarbonate below 18 mmol/L

blocks.text: DKA can occur with relatively normal glucose, particularly with SGLT2 inhibitors, pregnancy or prolonged fasting. This is called euglycaemic DKA.

items.text: **F – Fluids:** restore circulating volume with appropriate IV crystalloid.
**I – Insulin:** IV insulin according to protocol, once potassium safety has been assessed.
**P – Potassium:** monitor and replace according to serum concentration and local protocol.
**M – Monitor:** glucose, ketones, electrolytes, renal function, venous pH and fluid balance.
**T – Treat trigger:** infection, insulin omission or other precipitating illness.
Assess potassium before commencing insulin; severe hypokalaemia requires potassium correction before insulin.
Dextrose is added when glucose falls to the protocol threshold so insulin can continue until ketonaemia resolves.
Monitor for cerebral injury, particularly in children and adolescents.

blocks.text: HHS is characterised by severe hyperglycaemia, hyperosmolality and profound dehydration, usually with little or no significant ketoacidosis.

items.text: Calculated or measured osmolality ≥320 mOsm/kg, depending on the diagnostic criterion used.
Drugs such as corticosteroids and diuretics.

blocks.text: **Exam pearl:** HHS has a high risk of thromboembolism, acute kidney injury and neurological complications. Mixed DKA/HHS presentations occur.
Hypoglycaemia is generally defined as glucose below 3.9 mmol/L in a person with diabetes; clinically significant hypoglycaemia is below 3.0 mmol/L.

items.text: **D** – Diabetes medication, particularly insulin and sulfonylureas.
**S** – Severe liver disease, alcohol or endocrine deficiency.
Conscious and able to swallow: give approximately 15–20 g of fast-acting oral glucose, then recheck glucose after 15 minutes and repeat if still low.
Unconscious or unable to swallow: do not give oral fluids or food; use IV glucose or IM glucagon according to availability and protocol.
Once recovered, provide longer-acting carbohydrate if appropriate and investigate the cause.

blocks.text: **Exam pearl:** Always consider sulfonylurea-associated prolonged or recurrent hypoglycaemia, especially in renal impairment.

subsections.subsection_title: 9. Insulin types – RAPID, SHORT, INTERMEDIATE, LONG

rows: Mealtime insulin, often given before meals

items.text: Basal insulin: provides background insulin coverage.
Bolus insulin: covers meals and sometimes correction of hyperglycaemia.

blocks.text: **Exam pearl:** Insulin preparations are not interchangeable unit-for-unit without considering their pharmacokinetic profile and prescribing instructions.
Hypothyroidism is reduced thyroid hormone production, resulting in a general slowing of metabolic processes.

rows: Organ-specific autoimmune disease, especially Hashimoto thyroiditis
Withdrawal or inadequate thyroid hormone replacement

blocks.text: Other causes include congenital thyroid abnormalities, drugs such as lithium and amiodarone, and pituitary or hypothalamic disease.

items.text: **Y** – Your metabolism slows: fatigue and weight gain.
**O** – Ongoing cold intolerance, constipation and dry skin.

blocks.text: In central hypothyroidism, free T4 is low with an inappropriately low or normal TSH.
**Exam pearl:** TSH alone can be misleading in pituitary or hypothalamic disease. Always interpret it alongside free T4 when central disease is suspected.
Hyperthyroidism is excessive thyroid hormone synthesis and secretion. Thyrotoxicosis is the clinical state caused by excess circulating thyroid hormones, regardless of the source.

items.text: **S** – Supplement or drug-related causes, including iodine and amiodarone.

blocks.text: Useful additional tests include TSH-receptor antibodies, thyroid ultrasound and radionuclide uptake studies when appropriate.

rows: Vision problems from thyroid eye disease

Beta-blockers for symptomatic control where suitable.

Antithyroid drugs require appropriate pregnancy-specific selection.
Radioactive iodine is contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding.

Iodine administered after the antithyroid drug, according to protocol.

blocks.text: A goitre is enlargement of the thyroid gland. It may be diffuse or nodular, and thyroid function may be normal, increased or decreased.

Family history of thyroid cancer or relevant hereditary syndromes.
Fine-needle aspiration cytology when indicated by ultrasound risk category and size.

blocks.text: **Exam pearl:** Correct significant hypomagnesaemia when treating hypocalcaemia because magnesium deficiency can impair PTH secretion and action.

blocks.text: Addison disease is primary adrenal insufficiency due to adrenal cortical destruction or dysfunction.

blocks.text: **Important distinction:** Secondary adrenal insufficiency due to pituitary disease typically has low or inappropriately normal ACTH, and aldosterone is usually preserved.

blocks.text: **Exam pearl:** Normal serum potassium does not exclude primary hyperaldosteronism. Screening is particularly important in resistant hypertension and selected patients with adrenal incidentalomas.
Both conditions result from excess growth hormone (GH), usually due to a pituitary somatotroph adenoma.

items.text: Gigantism: GH excess before closure of the epiphyseal growth plates, causing excessive linear growth.
Acromegaly: GH excess after epiphyseal closure, causing enlargement of hands, feet and facial bones.
Visual field defects from tumour compression.
Oral glucose tolerance test – failure of GH suppression supports the diagnosis.

blocks.text: **Exam pearl:** IGF-1 is generally preferred to a random GH measurement because GH secretion is pulsatile.
A prolactinoma is a prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma.
Other features include erectile dysfunction, hypogonadism, reduced bone density, headache and visual field defects in large tumours.

Hypopituitarism is deficiency of one or more pituitary hormones.

blocks.text: **Exam pearl:** In combined pituitary hormone deficiency, assess and treat possible cortisol deficiency before starting thyroid hormone replacement, because thyroid replacement can precipitate adrenal crisis.
Diabetes insipidus (DI) causes excessive production of dilute urine due to impaired vasopressin action.

items.text: Central DI – inadequate production or release of vasopressin.
Nephrogenic DI – renal resistance to vasopressin.
Gestational DI – increased breakdown of vasopressin during pregnancy.
Primary polydipsia – excessive water intake, which can mimic DI.
**E** – Elevated serum sodium may occur if water intake is inadequate.
Supervised water deprivation and desmopressin testing when indicated.

blocks.text: **Exam pearl:** Water deprivation testing must be supervised. It is not a home test and can cause dangerous dehydration or hypernatraemia.
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion causes excess water retention and dilutional hyponatraemia.

items.text: **I** – Intracranial disease, e.g. stroke, infection or trauma.
